question: A 28-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after being found in a confused state on an interstate rest area in Florida. She is unable to recall her name, address, or any other information regarding her person. She denies being the woman on a Connecticut driver's license found in her wallet. A telephone call with the police department of her hometown reveals that she had been reported missing three days ago by her husband. When the husband arrives, he reports that his wife has had a great deal of stress at work lately and before she went missing, was anxious to tell her boss that she will not meet the deadline for her current project. She has had two major depressive episodes within the past 4 years that were treated with citalopram. She drinks one to two beers daily and sometimes more on weekends. She does not use illicit drugs. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Physical and neurological examinations show no abnormalities. On mental status exam, she is oriented only to time and place but not to person. Short-term memory is intact; she does not recognize her husband or recall important events of her life. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Stress at work -> Anxiety -> Dissociative amnesia with dissociative fugue -> 70% CHAIN: Major depressive episodes -> Treated with citalopram -> Dissociative amnesia with dissociative fugue -> 60% CHAIN: Alcohol consumption -> Impaired memory -> Dissociative amnesia with dissociative fugue -> 70%
enhanced_information: The most likely diagnosis for the 28-year-old woman presenting with memory loss and confusion is dissociative amnesia with dissociative fugue. This is supported by the chain linking stress at work, anxiety, and impaired memory to this condition. The evidence paths mentioning citalopram and its association with hysteria and dissociative disorders further support this diagnosis.
analysis: The most likely diagnosis for the 28-year-old woman presenting with memory loss and confusion is dissociative amnesia with dissociative fugue. This is supported by the chain linking stress at work, anxiety, and impaired memory to this condition. The evidence paths mentioning citalopram and its association with hysteria and dissociative disorders further support this diagnosis. Other differential diagnoses like depersonalization disorder, dissociative identity disorder, Korsakoff syndrome, and delirium do not align as well with the presented clinical scenario.
